 161 ## 6. Estimating the floor
 162 
 163 **Research.** Bayesian learning of the reservation price (Zeng and Sycara 1998), regression on the
 164 opponent's concession curve (Hou 2004), Gaussian-process prediction of its next offers (IAMhaggler,
 165 Williams et al. 2011). With three counters p1, p2, p3 and geometric decay, Aitken's formula gives
 166 the limit: `R = p3 - (p3 - p2)^2 / ((p3 - p2) - (p2 - p1))`. Known failure: when step ratios rise
 167 (slower than geometric) it underestimates the floor and pushes too hard. Every observed counter is
 168 a hard upper bound on the floor.
 169 
 170 **For us.** Useful as a secondary signal, not a stop rule: the bot stops on patience before its
 171 floor, so a floor estimate mostly tells us whether a relationship charge is near (stabilise,
 172 secure supply) and whether a large first concession means room (already `DEEP` in the policy).
 173 The relationship charge in a finished practice result gives the supplier's true margin and cost
 174 (`learnings.md`), which beats any curve fit for practice cases.
 175 
 176 ## 7. Procurement levers by supplier situation
 177 
 178 **Research** (practice literature: Kraljic 1983, consultancy and CIPS sources; conventions, not
 179 studies): classify the position first (leverage: compete and push price; bottleneck and strategic:
 180 secure supply and joint value); answer a price-increase letter with a line-item breakdown weighted
 181 by each driver's cost share; accept justified increases only index-linked or temporary; price
 182 payment terms at both sides' cost of money; index clauses with a deadband of 3 to 5 %, a lag,
 183 a cap, both directions and only the exposed cost share; threaten a second source only if it is
 184 real; agree chargebacks before the dispute. Preferred-customer research (Schiele et al.): suppliers
 185 reward attractive customers with capacity and price; forecast visibility and payment reliability
 186 are what they ask for most. Collaborative but assertive buyers realise more value (Vantage
 187 Partners survey, correlational).
 188 
 189 **Playbook**, joined with our persona signals (`learnings.md`, Persona signals):
 190 
 191 | Situation | Signal in the data | Give | Ask | Avoid |
 192 |---|---|---|---|---|
 193 | Cash short | "bank is watching", "pay earlier", cash discount | faster payment when its rate beats our 8 % (cash discounts imply 37 to 56 %/yr) | price | ignoring its ask when payment is fixed: say so and offer the next best currency |
 194 | Fully booked | "fully booked", "allocates volumes" | its lead time, a firm 24-month volume, forecast | price at its standard speed | deep anchors (P10 patience 0.015), paying overtime for speed we do not value |
 195 | Spare capacity | "second shift on hold" | volume, extra parts, long term | price | |
 196 | Price frozen | "no room on price", "price list applies to all" | nothing on price | payment days, contract length, freight, start date | price pushes (no move, only lost patience) |
 197 | Approval ladder | "above 2 % need the approval" | small steps (2 % or less), a reason the rep can forward to its boss | | one big ask that goes to a committee |
 198 | Index-driven distributor | material share in its quote, clause offered | contract length only with a clause we can live with | deadband, share limited to material, falling series only | taking a 0 % deadband clause on a rising series (P02: score 0) |
 199 | Price increase letter | letter above its drivers' index move | the index-weighted justified part, later start | notice period, start date, split | citing indices that rose (they confirm its case) |
 200 | Stabilise, near cost | own-plant should-cost close to the quote | the price with the lowest C incl. relationship charge | terms | squeezing below sustainable margin (charge grows with the square) |
 201 | Quality first | high scorecard ppm | | low ppm commitment, chargeback at least `cost_per_defect` | trading quality away for price unless C says so |

 203 ## 8. RFQs with two or three bidders
 204 
 205 **Research.** Competition is worth more than negotiating skill: one extra bidder beats an optimally
 206 negotiated deal (Bulow and Klemperer 1996). For complex, non-standard contracts, negotiation beats
 207 a pure price auction because terms differ per bidder (Bajari, McMillan and Tadelis 2009). One
 208 best-and-final round works; repeated ones teach bidders to hold back (practice sources).
 209 
 210 **For us.** The current design matches: compare bids on total C, cite the cheapest rival's real
 211 standing offer (a new argument every round), keep losing threads alive as the alternative.
 212 Additions: one explicit best-and-final message per bidder near the end, not several; push the
 213 bidder with the lowest C first and keep others warm with a question about capacity or delivery.
 214 P05 is at 0.83, so RFQs are not where the points are.

 216 ## 9. Writing for LLM counterparts
 217 
 218 **Research.** The largest AI negotiation competition (Vaccaro et al. 2025, about 120k to 180k
 219 negotiations): warm agents beat cold ones on deal rate, joint value and counterpart satisfaction;
 220 dominance claimed value but raised impasses; positivity, gratitude and questions predicted deals.
 221 Buyers are harder for LLMs than sellers, and splitting a coded offer generator from an LLM narrator
 222 lifted buyer deal rates from 27 % to 89 % (OG-Narrator, Xia et al. 2024): our architecture.
 223 Asking about interests improves joint outcomes even when only one side does it (Thompson 1991).
 224 Disappointment draws concessions, anger backfires on value disputes (Van Kleef). Objective
 225 criteria and trades over positions (Fisher and Ury). LLMs drift toward a user who argues a side
 226 (sycophancy rose from 50 to 79 % in one benchmark): a calm, reasoned position held over rounds
 227 can move them, which is persuasion, not injection.
 228 
 229 **Writing rules** for `buyer/writer.py` and the paragraph prompt in `buyer/llm.py`:
 230 
 231 1. Open with one sentence that acknowledges its last message, specifically (what it moved, what it
 232    asked for).
 233 2. Answer every request it made, even with no: "Payment terms are fixed in this agreement; what
 234    we can offer instead is ..." (P11).
 235 3. One or two reasons per message, each a checkable fact next to its ID; more reasons dilute.
 236 4. Frame every move as a trade: "If you can do X, we can do Y."
 237 5. Ask one open question about its constraints ("What would make a price near X work for your
 238    planning?"). No "why" questions.
 239 6. Express disappointment at the gap, never anger at the person.
 240 7. Give the rep a forwardable rationale for its boss: figure, source, what we give in return.
 241 8. Name our last step as last, once, and mean it.
 242 9. No urgency, budget, target or missing alternative; no threats; no fake rivals; nothing aimed at
 243    the bot's instructions.

Buyer Agent: How the System Works
  ​Oct 10, 2026      · ​@Julian

Our agent negotiates each case as a team of parallel thread negotiators under one case
coordinator: code prepares the case from data, checks every supplier fact, and sets every
term; the LLM only reads replies and writes e-mails.


Architecture




system architecture · offline preparation, live wave, thread negotiator loop

Personas and claims are built once before the final. During a wave, every supplier thread
loops reader → fact check → policy → writer → guard; only the code steps set numbers.


A case, step by step
 1. Wave starts. The wave runner sees the new cases and starts one case coordinator per
     case, up to 10 in parallel.
 2. Prepare (within 20 s). The coordinator opens the session and builds a case brief from
    data: costs (C_open, our alternative, target, walk-away), the lever table, a view of each
     supplier, market facts and a claim bank of verified arguments. Unknown suppliers or



                                                                                        Page 1 of 8

     parts go through the fallback cascade. A stance call proposes each supplier's
     negotiation parameters, clamped by code.
 3. Negotiate in parallel. One thread negotiator per supplier runs a loop each round:
      a. The reader turns the supplier's e-mail into signals and factual statements.
      b. The fact checker tests each statement against our data.
      c. The policy engine picks the next term sheets and claims, or decides to accept or
         walk.
      d. The writer turns that decision into an e-mail.
      e. The guard checks it and sends it.
 4. Close. The coordinator accepts the best sheet that keeps every must-have and beats
    our alternative, or walks away. It closes at the latest 90 s before the wave's cap.
 5. Learn. The full trace and what we learned about each supplier are stored for the next
     practice run.

term; the LLM only reads replies and writes e-mails.

system architecture · offline preparation, live wave, thread negotiator loop

Personas and claims are built once before the final. During a wave, every supplier thread
loops reader → fact check → policy → writer → guard; only the code steps set numbers.


A case, step by step
 1. Wave starts. The wave runner sees the new cases and starts one case coordinator per
     case, up to 10 in parallel.
 2. Prepare (within 20 s). The coordinator opens the session and builds a case brief from
    data: costs (C_open, our alternative, target, walk-away), the lever table, a view of each
     supplier, market facts and a claim bank of verified arguments. Unknown suppliers or

     parts go through the fallback cascade. A stance call proposes each supplier's
     negotiation parameters, clamped by code.
 3. Negotiate in parallel. One thread negotiator per supplier runs a loop each round:
      a. The reader turns the supplier's e-mail into signals and factual statements.
      b. The fact checker tests each statement against our data.
      c. The policy engine picks the next term sheets and claims, or decides to accept or

def complete_from_env():
    """(system, user) -> text with the team's model over an OpenAI-compatible chat completions
    endpoint (`LLM_BASE_URL`, `LLM_MODEL`, `LLM_API_KEY`, `LLM_EFFORT`), or None when not configured."""
    model, key = os.environ.get("LLM_MODEL"), os.environ.get("LLM_API_KEY")
    if not model or not key:
        return None
    base = os.environ.get("LLM_BASE_URL", "https://api.openai.com/v1").rstrip("/")
    client = httpx.Client(timeout=TIMEOUT_S, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"})

    effort = os.environ.get("LLM_EFFORT", "low")

    def complete(system, user):
        messages = [{"role": "system", "content": system}, {"role": "user", "content": user}]
        body = {"model": model, "messages": messages, "reasoning_effort": effort}
        r = client.post(f"{base}/chat/completions", json=body)
        r.raise_for_status()
        return r.json()["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]

    return complete
